utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Good morning. Good morning, Mrs. Strugar.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... that I will ask you whether you solemnly declare that you will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth when you give your evidence today.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you very much for that. Mr. Rodic.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Examined by Mr. Rodic:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mrs. Strugar. Can you state your full name.

utterances.speaker: KATICA STRUGAR
utterances.text: My name is Katica Strugar.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell us, please: Where and when were you born?

utterances.speaker: KATICA STRUGAR
utterances.text: I was born on the 23rd of August, 1934, in Novi Sad.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What are you by ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: KATICA STRUGAR
utterances.text: I am an ethnic Croat, Roman Catholic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where did your family live?

utterances.speaker: KATICA STRUGAR
utterances.text: My family lived in Serbia for a while. Later, my father -- we were quite many in our family. We were ten children, in fact. Five of us are still alive. We lived in Serbia. Then my father moved back to Croatia. We lived in Croatia for a while. And then we returned to Serbia again. When my father retired, he was a Dalmatian. Therefore, he wanted to go back to Croatia and he went back to Pula, which is where my parents are buried.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Madam, do you still have any brothers or sisters who are still alive?

utterances.speaker: KATICA STRUGAR
utterances.text: Yes. Three brothers and one sister. Two brothers and my sister live in Zagreb, and I have one brother who lives in Pula. About two months ago, I visited them, after 14 years, and I also went to my parents' grave.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Madam, can you tell us about your educational background, please.

utterances.speaker: KATICA STRUGAR
utterances.text: I completed secondary pharmaceutical education and that was my job later on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: After you completed your education, did you get a job, and when was that?

utterances.speaker: KATICA STRUGAR
utterances.text: That was back in 1954. I got a job in the Zemun hospital pharmacy. Soon after I met my husband.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How did you get to meet Pavle?

utterances.speaker: KATICA STRUGAR
utterances.text: Well, he too worked in Zemun at the time, and we used the same means of public transportation and we would see each other every day. And as we were travelling to work, we became closer.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When did you marry him?

utterances.speaker: KATICA STRUGAR
utterances.text: In 1957, in January, we got married in Pec.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was his job at the time?

utterances.speaker: KATICA STRUGAR
utterances.text: He had already been transferred to Valjevo.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So he was a member of the army?

utterances.speaker: KATICA STRUGAR
utterances.text: Yes, the JNA.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was his ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: KATICA STRUGAR
utterances.text: He was a Montenegrin by ethnicity.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was that an obstacle to your life together?

utterances.speaker: KATICA STRUGAR
utterances.text: No, certainly not. I can provide an intimate detail here. Once he met me, he said, "I want to meet your parents too." And I told him, "Well, there's one thing you must keep in mind. I'm a Croat." And then he answered, "Well, that's got nothing to do with it, does it? What matters is our love. And since you've told me this, I have to tell you something too. Do you know who you are marrying? Do you know I'm a military officer? Do you know that I took a vow to serve my country? Do you know that whenever I get a transfer to another possibly even distant place I'll just have to go, and this may be any place at all between Triglav in the north and Djevdjelija in the south." And I just told him, "I'll go with you anywhere, just anywhere."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Ms. Strugar, do you have any children?

utterances.speaker: KATICA STRUGAR
utterances.text: We have two sons, Predrag, who was born in 1958, and Nenad, who was born in 1966.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Throughout his military career, was Mr. Strugar transferred very often?

utterances.speaker: KATICA STRUGAR
utterances.text: Yes. Not only very often; all too often, I'd say. As soon as we were married, got married -- when we got married, we were in Valjevo, and then after that we were in Belgrade. After Belgrade, we had to go to Slovenia. He was assigned to Bovec, but we lived about 40 kilometres away from him, because that was the only place we could find any private accommodation. And I lived there with our eldest son, and it was on a military cot that I gave birth to our second child in 1966, Nenad. It was only a while later that we were allocated a flat in Bovec. I went there. But then we left Bovec for Kranj. From Kranj we had to go to Prokuplje

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That's the south of Serbia, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: KATICA STRUGAR
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. From Prokuplje, we were back in Belgrade, and then from Belgrade to Pirot, and then from Pirot to Zajecar, from Zajecar to Sabac, from Sabac to Belgrade, and from Belgrade to Podgorica. And this is something that I must point out. Regardless of whether we had a flat to live in or not, he always tried so hard. He did his best to keep the family together so we could spend time together at all times.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What about these many transfers? How many times did you have to move?

utterances.speaker: KATICA STRUGAR
utterances.text: I'd say about 20 times, because we were never given a flat, and he had to look for private accommodation so we could stay with him. This is something he always wanted.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Madam, what about your children? Did they go to the same school or did they have to change schools all the time?

utterances.speaker: KATICA STRUGAR
utterances.text: No. Especially my eldest son, he had to change seven different schools throughout his elementary education, and in terms of secondary education he went to three different schools. Therefore, he began his last grade of secondary school in Pirot and completed it in Zajecar. The same applies to my youngest son. He had to change schools about five times.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me, Madam: What is their educational background? That of your sons, I mean.

utterances.speaker: KATICA STRUGAR
utterances.text: My eldest son had completed two years of a school for economics, and then later he wanted to go to military academy. He completed military academy and also he completed a PE college. My youngest son completed a school for catering and tourism.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Every time your husband got a transfer, did you manage to hold on to a job throughout this time?

utterances.speaker: KATICA STRUGAR
utterances.text: No. It was often the case, for example, when we were in Slovenia, I was out of a job. I worked in Zemun. I worked in Valjevo. I worked while we were in Pirot, in Zajecar, in Sabac, and also in Belgrade. And that's where I finally met all the conditions for early retirement.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How long have you been married for, Madam?

utterances.speaker: KATICA STRUGAR
utterances.text: 47 years.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Pavle Strugar, what's he like as a husband and father?

utterances.speaker: KATICA STRUGAR
utterances.text: As a husband, very sensitive, very tender to me, especially since I've taken ill. He devoted every spare moment he had to take me to hospital for checks and examinations and to stick with me throughout this difficult time. He respected me, and I respected him back. He was a very good father to our children, very tender, but he could also be very strict when that was required. He wanted them to respect his every word. And he wanted to have the final say, after all, especially when they were young boys and he would usually tell them by what time they had to come back in. There was no way they could have gone against that. They had to comply with what he said.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In addition to his regular job with the army, did he also try to pursue specialised studies?

utterances.speaker: KATICA STRUGAR
utterances.text: He was not an overly ambitious man, not in a bad way. He just worked hard to create a future for his family. He worked hard. He pursued specialised courses and training to make himself a better professional and he earned everything that he got.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did Pavle like his job?

utterances.speaker: KATICA STRUGAR
utterances.text: Very much so. He very much liked his job, and he respected his job.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did he keep job and family apart or was his family affected because of the kind of work he did?

utterances.speaker: KATICA STRUGAR
utterances.text: No. He kept the two apart and we were never affected. When he came home, he dedicated himself to me and our children, and he wanted his children to do lots of sports. He was a very proficient skier, and when we still lived in Slovenia, he wanted our children to learn to ski, and they were very successful in that. They won distinctions and medals in different competitions. Therefore, he wanted his children to do lots of sports and he spent all the spare time that he had with me and our children. Now, as for his work, I never talked to him about it. It was just something we didn't talk about at home.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You've told us that Pavle is a Montenegrin by ethnicity and you are a Croat yourself. In your relationship, have you ever noticed that he showed any hostility to someone who was of a different ethnicity than himself?

utterances.speaker: KATICA STRUGAR
utterances.text: No. That was never the case. That's not the sort of man he is. He has a mixed ethnic background in terms of his family, and so do I. Some of my relatives are Serbs, some are Croats. He has both Muslims and Slovenes in his family. It was a mix. All he ever tried was to be an honourable man.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How did he treat your family?

utterances.speaker: KATICA STRUGAR
utterances.text: With respect. He was and he still is dearly loved by them. They always ask questions about him, and now that I was in Croatia, they send him greetings and their love. They want this to come to a speedy end so we can spend the rest of our lives, what little remains, in peace. And there is another thing I wish to say. Every time we went on vacation, he wanted us to spend half the vacation with my family and the other half with his family. That's how it was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What do you know about Pavle's family?

utterances.speaker: KATICA STRUGAR
utterances.text: I've been part of that family for a very long time, so I know quite a bit. He also comes from a big family. They were 12 children in his family. Three of his brothers got killed in World War II, in the national liberation struggle. They were partisans in World War II. Three of his sisters also took part in World War II, and one of them was awarded a badge of courage. It's a working family, a family of honest people. They accepted me as if I were their daughter.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Back in 1990 and 1991, what was Pavle's reaction to what was going on in the Socialist Federative Republic of Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: KATICA STRUGAR
utterances.text: Well, as I said, precisely on account of our mixed backgrounds, what started to happen was a tragedy, for him and for me, and we couldn't even assume back at the time what would happen. But we were really afraid and we were really concerned.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In 1991, did Pavle go to the front?

utterances.speaker: KATICA STRUGAR
utterances.text: Yes. He had no choice. He had taken a vow to serve his country.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was that what he said to you at the time?

utterances.speaker: KATICA STRUGAR
utterances.text: That's precisely what he said. He said, "My love, I have to go. Take heart." We just wanted to believe that the whole thing would settle down gradually and that the end would not be so painful.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell us when Pavle retired?

utterances.speaker: KATICA STRUGAR
utterances.text: He retired in 2000 and -- I can't remember the exact year. I think it was 2001, but I can't be sure about this. I'm sorry. I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Fair enough. Thank you. Did Pavle have any health problems?

utterances.speaker: KATICA STRUGAR
utterances.text: Yes. He did too, especially with his kidneys. There's something else I can tell you. Whenever he was the one to be ill, he wanted to spare me the trouble. He wanted to cope on his own. He had had about ten stone kidneys extracted and he knew what enormous pain that was. And he just wanted to be shut up in a room before the emergency arrived. He wanted to spare us watching him in pain.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me, Mrs. Strugar: Where do you live now?

utterances.speaker: KATICA STRUGAR
utterances.text: I live in Podgorica. But in view of my health condition, I cannot live on my own. There always has to be someone by my side. So our children take turns and they bring me to Belgrade. We have four wonderful grandchildren. They have very small apartments, 54 square metres each. But it's not too small for us. We want to overcome this as soon as possible.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me: Do your sons have jobs?

utterances.speaker: KATICA STRUGAR
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me, Mrs. Strugar: What is the condition of your own health?

utterances.speaker: KATICA STRUGAR
utterances.text: Since 1981 or 1982, I have severe health problems. I have glaucoma on both eyes. I got ill while we were in Sabac, then he urgently transferred me too Belgrade to the military academy where surgery was performed on both eyes immediately, and after that I had two more interventions. Unfortunately, I lost my left eye. As for the right eye -- I'm terribly sorry. I'm under therapy all the time, and I have to go for check-ups.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the usher please distribute a document.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mrs. Strugar --

utterances.speaker: KATICA STRUGAR
utterances.text: Please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can we go ahead?

utterances.speaker: KATICA STRUGAR
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me: What's the situation like with your other eye now? Is it damaged?

utterances.speaker: KATICA STRUGAR
utterances.text: Yes. I had surgery recently, cataract, and I went for eye correction less than a month ago. My eyesight was corrected. I have to go for check-ups all the time. And I put a lens in my left eye because I have an inflammation there, the cornea.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the usher please put the original document there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mrs. Strugar, could you please take a look at this and tell us whether these are your medical findings. Are these the findings of your doctor?

utterances.speaker: KATICA STRUGAR
utterances.text: Oh, yes, Professor Kuljaca. He actually performed surgery on my eyes and I went to be treated by him only recently. He did this eyesight correction. He has been monitoring the condition of my health and this is the original document.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. We won't be needing it any longer.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me, Mrs. Strugar: Due to your health problems, was Pavle always by your side?

utterances.speaker: KATICA STRUGAR
utterances.text: Yes, all the time. And we sought help everywhere. He took me everywhere, just in order to help me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me, please: Due to your poor eyesight, do you need an escort in order to be able to move about?

utterances.speaker: KATICA STRUGAR
utterances.text: Yes. I can't walk on my own.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me, please: How did Pavle Strugar react in October 2001, when the indictment against him was made public?

utterances.speaker: KATICA STRUGAR
utterances.text: That was very painful for us, for the entire family. When this became public, many people gave him advice: Do this, do that. After having slept on it, or rather, not having slept on it throughout the night, he called me and he said, "Dear, I have to tell you that I want to surrender this very minute and go before this Honourable Court, to prove my innocence." I accepted that, as always. I made no comment. I trust this Honourable Court and I believe that the truth will prevail.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me, Mrs. Strugar: Did you stay in Podgorica on your own?

utterances.speaker: KATICA STRUGAR
utterances.text: Yes. Pavle has a nephew there, the son of his late brother, and for a while they were by my side, and then our sons came.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me, finally: Let me just ask you one more thing. You've been married for a long time with Pavle. Have you ever heard anything bad about him from anyone?

utterances.speaker: KATICA STRUGAR
utterances.text: No. On the contrary. I told you how many apartments we changed, owned by landlords, owned by the army, wherever. As a family, we were welcomed everywhere, and everybody respected us. We never had any conflicts with anyone, anywhere.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mrs. Strugar, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I have concluded my examination-in-chief, and I would just like to tender this document, the medical findings of Mrs. Strugar. Could it please be assigned a number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, the number will be D107.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Ms. Somers.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Just a very brief couple of practical questions, Your Honour. Cross-examined by Ms. Somers:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Good morning, Ms. Strugar.

utterances.speaker: KATICA STRUGAR
utterances.text: Good morning Mrs. Somers.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Nice to see you. Mrs. Strugar, I wonder if you could just help me understand about where your treatment for your eye condition is taking place. Is it -- I see the seal of the letter. There's a stamp on the letter. It says "Belgrade." Are you being treated regularly in Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: KATICA STRUGAR
utterances.text: Yes. When I live in Podgorica, I have a doctor there as well who comes every now and then. This is this doctor, Professor Kuljaca, who performed surgery on my eyes, so I'll always under medical control.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Do you still -- if I understand correctly, you still do live in Belgrade, you have your house in Belgrade. Are your boys living part time in Belgrade -- I'm sorry. In Podgorica. Excuse me. You still have your house in Podgorica? That's your -- where you really live?

utterances.speaker: KATICA STRUGAR
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. Where you saw us. That is locked up now. There's no one there, because I cannot live on my own. I'm staying with either one of the boys or the other one. I told you, both my sons have two children each. They're big children. And their apartments are 54 square metres only. So I stay with them, but never mind, it's not too small for us.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But that's in Podgorica or in Belgrade? Have they moved completely to Podgorica or are they in Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: KATICA STRUGAR
utterances.text: Yes. They live in Belgrade, with their families.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you're spending most of your time now in Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: KATICA STRUGAR
utterances.text: For the most part, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you for clearing that up. Besides this trip, in addition to this particular trip that you have made to come see your husband, have you been outside of the former Yugoslavia before? Have you ever travelled foreign before this trip today?

utterances.speaker: KATICA STRUGAR
utterances.text: No. No. No, unfortunately.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do your sons have automobiles? Are they able to transport you when you need to be transported, or do you have to rely on trams or --

utterances.speaker: KATICA STRUGAR
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. Yes. They do, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And there are -- their wives are also assisting in whatever assistance you might need, your daughters-in-law help out?

utterances.speaker: KATICA STRUGAR
utterances.text: Oh, indeed, yes. I'm on very good terms, exceptionally good terms with my daughters-in-law. They're very attentive to me and their children are, so there are no problems in that respect.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Your sons, you indicated, are presently not working. What are their professions, if they have professional training, or what is their vocation?

utterances.speaker: KATICA STRUGAR
utterances.text: I've told you that our older son completed the military academy and the college of physical education, and every now and then he has a part-time job teaching. The younger son also has part-time jobs, but neither sons -- neither one of my sons have permanent jobs.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are your daughters-in-law working?

utterances.speaker: KATICA STRUGAR
utterances.text: One daughter-in-law is a pharmacist, my older son's wife. She went to university and has a university degree in pharmaceutics, and the younger one is still looking for a job. She has also applied -- she is also registered with the bureau of unemployment.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Q. I observe that one of your sons accompanied you to The Hague today. I'm sure you're very happy about that. Has -- have your boys been outside? Have they travelled foreign besides the trip that one of your sons has made today? Or is this the first time either of your sons has been outside Yugoslavia, or the former Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: KATICA STRUGAR
utterances.text: Well, I know they went skiing. I told you that, that the younger son went with my sister, because my sister has no children. Then she took him to Italy. The older son was in the Tatra mountains with skiers. But otherwise, no, they didn't.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mrs. Strugar. There's nothing more I have to ask you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you too, Mrs. Somers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Rodic, is there anything further?

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I have no additional questions. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mrs. Strugar, thank you very much for coming to The Hague and for the evidence you've given to assist the Tribunal. That concludes your evidence. You can just stay seated for a little while and we'll attend to one or two other matters, and then you will be able to spend a moment here with your husband. Mr. Rodic, what is the next position with the next witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, unfortunately, the Defence cannot bring in the next witness who was planned for today due to health problems. We had our last contact with the witness this morning, before entering the courtroom, and he was waiting to go and see a doctor. So during the course of the day, we hope that the witness's health condition will improve after he sees the doctor and after he receives some therapy. Then perhaps the witness may be ready to appear before the Honourable Trial Chamber tomorrow. We tried last night too. We went to see him. But he had these health problems. He pointed out what the health problems were, so he could not really speak to us properly last night in order to be able to appear in Court this morning. The situation continued until this morning. This morning, before entering the courtroom, we contacted him. His condition remained unchanged, and he was waiting to go and see a doctor. That's the last witness we have here in The Hague, the last witness who was planned for this week in The Hague, except for tomorrow. What we have planned for tomorrow, the videolink witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I take it, first, that you see no prospect of the witness being available this afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, right now, at this moment, I really cannot say anything about that. I can take it upon myself to contact the witness after the break to see what the result of the medical examination was, to see what the situation is, and to ask him. But you will understand that I wouldn't want to force him to do anything. It really would depend on his health. But I will certainly contact him, and I will notify the Honourable Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you for that, Mr. Rodic. We would appreciate that, in particular because your phone call will determine whether the accused needs to just continue to wait here or whether he can go back to the Detention Centre, and I can well expect that he would be much happier going back to the Detention Centre. So the sooner you can get word to Ms. Musser, the better on that. The second matter is that the witness tomorrow certainly won't take the whole of the morning session, by the look of things.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I think that during the first session, probably not the entire session, the Defence will probably take an hour, an hour and 15 minutes, and we'll do our best to complete the examination-in-chief within that time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Well, if your witness from today may be able to be heard then tomorrow morning. The effect of all of this, of course, is that it will be necessary for you to be -- and Mr. Petrovic, to be extremely focused and disciplined with the witnesses to come and get to the points that really matter and not worry about the others. Because we've got to make up time. Ms. Somers, I saw you half to your feet.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Your Honours. First of all, we certainly hope that the witness is feeling better. We share the concern for his health. In the event he is suddenly produced, we have not, of course, had a proofing summary. I understand the proofing did not take place. So the Chamber knows we received a call last night about 10.00 in my office from a member of the Defence team, indicating what the problem was and indicating there had been no proofing. So we are assuming hopefully everything is fine with his health, we still do not have any real direction as to whether or not there will be something beyond the very limited 65 ter description. Also, I apologise for taking the time of everybody, including Mrs. Strugar, but the order of witnesses for next week needs -- we need to know. We are obviously under the same time constraints as everyone. We, in an accommodation to the Defence, went with less time than is normally granted under Rule 94 bis, and so if there's going to be any movement above and beyond what is in the 94 bis statement for purposes of direct, it would be very helpful for us to know, because we are, as is everyone, advancing at rapid speed to try to accommodate the deadline. Rapid speed in quotation marks.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I was going to say, by the standards I'm used to, a snail would be galloping past us.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Diplomacy is part of my job, Your Honour. I wanted to just indicate that once we have the schedule, the order, and if in fact the Defence has indicated there may be some witnesses who will not be presented, if we could know who not. There's a tremendous amount of work and preparation. All of us are calling each other at very bizarre hours of the night. So we're all working the same hours. It would be helpful and then we would be able to bring everything to a -- I think a good conclusion. But just through that kind of orderly process. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: The ultimate concern in all of this is that it will make an enormous difference to the strain on the accused if we can conclude the evidence before the break. Because if that doesn't occur, the trial will necessarily expand out by at least a month longer. And it's for that reason that we are urging both sides to be extremely disciplined and focused in their attention to what are the material issues in the evidence. Mr. Rodic, if the concerns of the Prosecution to know the order of witnesses for next week, and if there are any significant changes from the information they presently have can be kept closely in mind, and if you can make that information available to them as soon as you have it, it would facilitate their work in preparing at very short notice and enhance the prospects of a satisfactory completion of the evidence in good time. We will adjourn now. Whether we are able to resume later today will depend upon the message that you give to Ms. Musser. And you will have heard my words. The sooner that's known, decisions can be made about the accused and having to just wait around here. We propose now to adjourn. It's possible that we could resume today if the witness is available. Otherwise, it will be at 9.00 in the morning. The videolink will be first, and if the witness of today can then be heard, we will be in a position to do that. When we adjourn, I'd appreciate it if security would allow a little time when Mrs. Strugar is with the accused just in the Court there. Thank you. We will adjourn.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.
